about.title: Fire and the changing body
about.length_note: About 25 minutes. Fire has a lot to cover: three kinds of fire control, three sites that each get two dates, daily life, Homo erectus, and two open debates. The beats are short and each has a check question, so the class runs a little longer than a bare outline would. It can be split in two at the 'daily life' beat.

say.text: Welcome to class four: Fire and the changing body. Today we ask how fire changed daily life, and when people first took control of it.

show.text: Fire and the changing body

say.text: Last class was stone tools. Fire is another tool, and a strange one: you can't hold it, and it can run away from you. The original hot topic.

show.text: Fire: a tool you can't hold

say.text: First idea: using fire. That means making use of a fire nature started, like a wildfire. Some researchers think our ancestors first met fire this way.

show.text: 1. Using fire

say.text: Second idea: keeping fire. That means carrying flames somewhere else and feeding them so they don't go out.

show.text: 2. Keeping fire

say.text: Third idea: making fire. That means starting a flame yourself, on demand. One way is striking flint against a mineral called pyrite to throw sparks.

show.text: 3. Making fire

say.text: So there are three steps: use it, keep it, make it. Let's check you have them straight.

show.text: Using: borrow a natural fire | Keeping: carry it and feed it | Making: start it yourself

ask.q: A group carries a burning branch from a wildfire into a cave and feeds it until it dies out. Which step is this?
wrong: Making fire
Cooking food
Nothing, because fire can't be carried
ask.why: They didn't start the flame, but they moved it and fed it. That is keeping fire, not making it.

say.text: Why does this matter? Because 'when did people control fire?' has a different answer for each step. Keep the three steps in mind all class.

show.text: Which step are we talking about?

say.text: How do we know about fire at all? Look for a hearth: a spot where fires were lit again and again. Fire leaves ash, burned bone, burned seeds and wood, and scorched stone.

show.text: Hearth: a place where fire was lit, again and again

say.text: Here is an example from a site we'll visit soon: pieces of flint scorched by fire. Burned seeds and wood were found close by.

show.text: Three small pieces of flint, scorched and discoloured by burning, from Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in Israel.

say.text: Here's the trouble. Wildfires also leave burned ground, and the traces can be tiny and subtle. Archaeologists have to be careful.

show.text: Wildfires leave burned traces too | Old fire traces are subtle and hard to detect

say.text: So what clues help? Burned pieces in tight clusters, fires repeated in the same spot, burning deep inside a cave, and signs of heat.

show.text: Dense clusters, not random scatter | Repeated fires in one spot | Burning deep inside a cave | Evidence of heating (about 500 degrees C in one case)

ask.q: Burned flints lie in tight clusters, in the same spots, across thousands of years. Which explanation fits best?
ask.right: People lit fires at those spots again and again
wrong: One wildfire swept through once
The wind blew the flints into piles
Nobody can say anything at all
ask.why: A single bush fire would scatter burned pieces at random. Dense clusters in repeated spots point to hearths.

say.text: Now three sites, and each gets two dates. First, when people used fire there. Second, when archaeologists found it. Our first site is Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa.

show.text: The inside of Wonderwerk Cave, looking toward the back: a long, narrow tube in a hillside, with layered deposits being excavated.

say.text: Wonderwerk is a tube-shaped cave about 140 metres long, in the Kuruman Hills. Its two dates are very far apart.

show.text: Fire burned in the cave: about 1.79 to 1.07 million years ago | Found: 1940s, diggers taking cave dung for fertiliser expose old tools | 1970s-1990s: Peter Beaumont excavates | 2012: fire traces published | June 2026: older fire traces reported

say.text: The 2012 team found microscopic wood ash and burned bone with stone tools, in a layer about a million years old. The bone had been heated to around 500 degrees Celsius.

show.text: Wonderwerk 2012: ash, burned bone, tools, about 1 million years ago

say.text: Notice the odd part. Beaumont had dug up this material long before. It took microscopes to recognise it as fire, so it was found twice. The team saw no sign of wind, water or wildfire.

show.text: Dug up once, recognised as fire decades later

say.text: In June 2026 a new study reported fire traces in older layers, between about 1.07 and 1.79 million years ago. It used the glow of burned bone as a test.

show.text: 1,790,000 years ago (upper end of the 2026 range)

say.text: But the team does not think these people lit the fire. Michael Chazan describes it as collecting a fire from the landscape. He says fire use was probably only occasional.

show.text: Kept, not made

ask.q: What do the Wonderwerk researchers think the early people did with fire?
ask.right: They carried and maintained fire from natural wildfires, but probably didn't light it
wrong: They made fire with flint and pyrite
They baked fish in an earth oven
They never used fire at all
ask.why: The researchers describe collecting a natural fire and keeping it going, not starting one.

say.text: Second site: Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, in Israel's Jordan Valley. About 780,000 years ago it was the shore of an ancient lake, called paleo-Lake Hula.

show.text: Northern Israel, south of the Hula Valley, along the Jordan River; the site lies on the corridor between Africa and Eurasia.

say.text: Again two dates. People lived there about 780,000 years ago. Archaeologists have studied it since the 1930s, with big digs in 1989 to 1997.

show.text: People camp on the lake shore: about 780,000 years ago, returning over tens of thousands of years | Found: investigated since the 1930s | Excavated 1989-1997 under Naama Goren-Inbar | Fire evidence: Smithsonian lists 2004

say.text: The fire evidence there is burned flint in dense clusters, plus burned seeds and wood. That points to hearths used again and again.

show.text: Gesher: clusters of burned flint = hearths

say.text: In 2022 researchers reported something more: teeth of a large carp-like fish near those burned-flint clusters, showing it was cooked. Cooking here means heating food at a controlled temperature.

show.text: Cooked fish, about 780,000 years ago

ask.q: What was the evidence for cooking at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov?
ask.right: Fish teeth near burned-flint clusters, showing the fish had been heated
wrong: Clay pots with stew inside
A written recipe
Burnt loaves of bread
ask.why: The cooking evidence came from fish teeth found within or next to the burned-flint clusters.

say.text: Before this, firm evidence of cooking was only about 170,000 years old. That is a big jump back, and it shows how much depends on new methods.
Third site: Barnham, in Suffolk, England. About 400,000 years ago it was the edge of a stream-fed pond, with grass and woodland around it.

show.text: An old clay pit in Suffolk, where archaeologists dig deep trenches into the sediments of an ancient dried-up pond.

say.text: Its two dates again. People lit fires there about 400,000 years ago, probably early Neanderthals. Workers found stone tools in the early 1900s, and the fire evidence took until 2025.

show.text: Fires lit: about 400,000 years ago, probably early Neanderthals | Found: stone tools first noticed in the early 1900s | Excavations 1989-1994 | First pyrite fragment found 2017 | Published in Nature, December 2025

say.text: The evidence: baked earth forming a hearth, heat-shattered flint hand axes, and two pieces of iron pyrite. Pyrite throws sparks when struck with flint. The team thinks it was brought in on purpose.

show.text: Baked earth hearth | Heat-cracked flint hand axes | Two fragments of iron pyrite

ask.q: Why does the pyrite at Barnham matter?
ask.right: It makes sparks and was probably brought to the site, suggesting people made fire rather than only keeping it
wrong: It was a food the people cooked
It was a stone used to build walls
It proves they lived in houses
ask.why: Pyrite plus flint makes sparks. If it was carried in, that points to deliberate fire-making.

say.text: Here are the claims side by side. The older ones are about keeping fire. Only the youngest, Barnham, is argued to show fire being made.

show.text: Claims for early fire, in years ago

ask.q: In the chart, which claim is argued to show fire being made, not only kept?
wrong: Wonderwerk Cave, about 1.79 million years ago
Wonderwerk Cave, about 1 million years ago
Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, about 780,000 years ago
ask.why: Barnham is the one with the pyrite and flint. The researchers say they have the earliest evidence of making fire.

say.text: Now daily life. What did a fire give a family? Four things: warmth, protection, light, and cooked food.

show.text: Warmth | Protection | Light | Cooked food

say.text: Fire gave comfort in the cold and safety from predators. At night it gave light. People could gather round it to socialise and share food and news.

show.text: A small group seated close around a glowing campfire at night, with darkness beyond.

say.text: Then cooking. Cooked food is easier to digest, so the body gets more energy from it. Great apes spend four to seven hours a day just chewing.

show.text: Cooking: easier to digest, more energy

ask.q: How does cooking help the body?
ask.right: It makes food easier to digest, so more energy is gained from the same food
wrong: It removes the need to eat
It makes teeth grow back
It makes food colder and lighter
ask.why: Cooking improves digestibility and energy intake.

say.text: Now the body. Homo erectus appeared about 1.8 million years ago. It was the first of our relatives with human-like proportions: shorter arms and longer legs for its torso.

show.text: Homo erectus: a human-like body

say.text: Its brain was bigger than earlier Homo. Estimates vary, but sources put the average near 900 cc or more, and its teeth were smaller than Homo habilis.

show.text: Average braincase size (cc)

say.text: A fair warning: the body grew too. Compared with body size, the Homo erectus brain was not much bigger than Homo habilis.

show.text: Bigger brain, but a bigger body too

say.text: Big brains burn lots of energy. The 'expensive tissue' idea, from Leslie Aiello and Peter Wheeler in 1995, says a smaller gut can free up energy for a bigger brain.

show.text: Expensive tissue hypothesis: smaller gut, bigger brain

ask.q: What trade-off does the expensive tissue idea describe?
ask.right: A smaller gut saves energy that a bigger brain can use
wrong: A bigger gut makes a bigger brain
A bigger brain needs less food
Smaller teeth always mean a smaller brain
ask.why: The idea is a trade-off between two costly organs, the gut and the brain.

say.text: Where does fire fit? Richard Wrangham argues cooking was the real breakthrough, fuelling the brain. His timeline puts it around when Homo erectus appeared. That is where the argument starts.

show.text: Wrangham's cooking hypothesis

say.text: First debate: when did regular fire use begin? Three views. Very early, for Homo erectus. Around a million years ago or 780,000. Or only about 400,000 to 300,000 years ago.

show.text: Early: about 1.8 million years ago (Wrangham; hints at Wonderwerk) | Middle: about 1 million to 780,000 years ago (Wonderwerk 2012, Gesher) | Late: regular use from about 400,000 to 300,000 years ago (Roebroeks and Villa, for Europe)

say.text: Wil Roebroeks and Paola Villa reviewed European sites. They found early people reached cold northern Europe without regular fire. They don't rule out earlier fire, but say it wasn't habitual.

show.text: Habitual fire in Europe: about 400,000-300,000 years ago

say.text: Rick Potts adds a warning. Saying early people 'must have' used fire is not evidence. In his view only physical remains, like hearths and burned tools, can set the date.

show.text: 'Must have' is not evidence

say.text: Second debate: did cooking drive bigger brains? Aiello and Wheeler think energy-rich animal foods like marrow and brain did it. Skeptics also say the archaeology of fire doesn't reach back far enough.

show.text: Cooking explains it (Wrangham) | Meat and marrow explain it (Aiello and Wheeler); fire evidence too late (skeptics)

ask.q: Why do some experts doubt that cooking drove bigger brains in Homo erectus?
ask.right: Archaeological evidence for controlled fire doesn't clearly reach that far back, and eating more animal food could explain the same changes
wrong: Because nobody ever cooked food
Because Homo erectus had a smaller brain than Homo habilis
Because cooking makes food harder to digest
ask.why: Skeptics point to gaps in the fire record and to meat as another explanation. Wrangham answers that no other time fits the body changes so well.

say.text: So what is safe to say? Fire was used long before we can show it was made. The oldest claims are about keeping wildfire. Fire-making is shown from about 400,000 years ago.

show.text: Earliest claims: keeping natural fire, probably occasional | Fire-making: argued from about 400,000 years ago | Cooking and brain size: still debated

ask.q: Which statement is the safest summary?
ask.right: Fire use probably began long before fire-making can be shown, and scientists still debate when regular use began
wrong: Everyone agrees people controlled fire 2 million years ago
Cooking is proven to have caused our big brains
Homo erectus lit fires with pyrite
ask.why: The evidence for early fire is real but contested. Making fire is shown much later than keeping it, and the cooking-and-brains link is still argued.

say.text: Next class: leaving Africa the first time. Keep today's question in mind: how did people cope in colder lands, with or without regular fire?

show.text: Next: Leaving Africa the first time

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Homo erectus appears in the fossil record. The species is dated from about 1.8 million to 112,000 years ago.
People at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov were living on a corridor between Africa and Eurasia, a route later important in the out-of-Africa story.
Early Neanderthals lived in the region. Fossils of about the same age come from Swanscombe in Kent and Atapuerca in Spain.
Before the 2022 Gesher fish study, this was the date of the firmest evidence of cooking, by early Homo sapiens and Neanderthals.
Neanderthals in northern France made fire. This was the oldest known fire-making evidence until Barnham in 2025.

other_side.claim: Fire traces at Wonderwerk Cave up to about 1.8 million years ago show Homo erectus controlled fire.
other_side.other_view: The study team does not claim these people lit fires. Michael Chazan says they collected a fire from the landscape, and that use was probably only occasional. Wil Roebroeks, who was not involved, says any fire use was marginal, not habitual. Rick Potts says a 'must have' argument is not evidence.

other_side.claim: Barnham shows fire-making about 400,000 years ago, the earliest known.
other_side.other_view: The authors say fire-making probably did not begin at Barnham. Wil Roebroeks, though, thinks the claim stretches the evidence, and no fire-lighting tools with friction marks have been found there yet.

other_side.claim: Cooking made bigger brains possible, starting with Homo erectus (Richard Wrangham).
other_side.other_view: Aiello and Wheeler agree that smaller guts go with bigger brains, but think energy-rich animal foods caused it. Skeptics say the archaeology of controlled fire doesn't support such early cooking. Wrangham replies that no other period fits the body changes so well.

other_side.claim: Early people could only have settled cold northern lands with fire.
other_side.other_view: Many archaeologists have thought so. Roebroeks and Villa's review of European sites suggests early people got there without habitual fire, and that regular fire use there dates from about 300,000 to 400,000 years ago.
